Ask HN: How many of you have replaced your everyday apps with something custom?
stories.text:
This question isn't specific to vibe-coded apps, I was just curious how many people are using bespoke everyday software, for things like a file explorer, terminal, maybe mail client, text editor etc.

Down the line I had planned on writing my own terminal, text editor and file explorer, but had too many other high priority projects and hadn't gotten around to it yet, and probably wouldn't for another year.

Playing with Claude, after only...six prompts, I have my ideal custom terminal...kitty graphics, iterm style tmux integration, transparency, renaming tabs, session support, other small stuff; it's tailored exactly to my workstyle and aesthetic tastes, and so far is working amazingly.

I see why so much vibe-coded stuff gets released - because it's exciting to share having brought your vision to life. If I had written this pre-AI, I'd be proud of it and want to share, but now, if it only takes six prompts to generate, I'm not sure there would be a point?

Show HN: Taskless, turn AGENTS.md and PR comments into runnable checks
stories.text:
Hey HN, I'm Jakob, the solo dev and founder behind Taskless.

I got tired of my AGENTS.md files being ignored or forgotten a half dozen turns into conversations. I also remembered reading someone here on HN saying we weren't using nearly enough syntax trees in our code checks. This is the result.

Taskless gives you powerful syntax tree tools with human verifiable fixtures. The CLI is MIT licensed, so running the CLI, onboarding, rule writing, and running the underlying ast-grep & Vale checks are all local. You can give it a try with:

npx @taskless/cli

and then asking your agent to "onboard with Taskless".

Under the hood, the CLI works with your agent to read your PR review comments, fixup commits, and agent files. It takes things that keep recurring and turns them into the simplest code-level enforcement that can prevent the issue going forward. By choosing code over an LLM for the runtime, there's no model once code is generated. The checks can then be committed to your codebase and enforced. I'm particularly proud of how determinism is mixed into the onboarding flow. Any time the CLI can give the agent information without letting the agent wandering the codebase, the CLI does. It results in a more consistent experience with far fewer errors. Anonymous telemetry can be disabled outright by setting DO_NOT_TRACK=1 or TASKLESS_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 in your environment (it collects CLI version, OS, the repo's org/owner, and a bit about the repository it's running in).

When the agent's done, it creates a report you can share around to show everyone there's a better way to control the output of agentic coding tools. I thought I'd include a few here from some of my favorite repos.

- Effect: https://tskl.es/gh/Effect-TS/effect/20261104/1g4gRoMmoADlysg... I specifically liked Effect because effect-bot is in the PRs fixing bugs and writing docs for the team, and they already use oxlint plugins and a TypeScript language service plugin.

- Sentry: https://tskl.es/gh/getsentry/sentry/20261016/1ZyMPva1BzaHaa5... Sentry's all open source, and David Cramer's tweeted a lot about determinism, especially now that the team is using Junior to ship code via Slack chat.

- n8n: https://tskl.es/gh/n8n-io/n8n/20261026/1C3I3yVjFyfxNFEpl4qFA... n8n has more AI driven code than the other two repos and is a good example of how bad it can get when the determinism isn't in place. Since agents tend to copy what they see from related files, problems propagate quickly.

I'd love to hear what you're doing today to keep agents behaving, or if you do kick the tires, I'd love the honest feedback.

stories.text: I built it because it's very hard to keep up with all the new CVEs coming out. The main problem is I don't know which ones apply to my computer, projects or our infra. So I built pantry to make it easier to figure out what actually needs to be patched, if it even can be, and how to do it quickly. It has lots of features so I think it would be helpful for other people so we just open sourced it as my first product at my new AI co because we're using it internally to secure some of our agentic runtimes and our own infra.

Show HN: It's now easy to install Linux on an Android Phone – Android2linux
stories.text:
Hey HN!

One of my biggest dreams (really) was to have a Linux phone. I tried to install on some phones in the past, even the ones that would be marked as compatible and it was always so difficult that I couldn't really do it. Yesterday I decided to try again, this time using Claude to do most of the work. A couple hours later it runs postmarketOS as my second phone: 4G, SMS, a terminal, SSH.

It took two fixes. U-Boot didn't recognise my phone model, so I patched 14 bytes of its device-tree match strings. Then the modem wasn't working, because the packaged TFTP server that lends the modem a folder mishandled its file-size queries but an upstream build fixed it.

The repo is what came out of it: guides for any phone (but specific just for my xiaomi), an agent skill that follows the same method and safety rules, notes per phone, and web apps reworked for a phone screen (WhatsApp Web for desktop with a one-pane layout).

What doesn't work (in this phone of mine): no charger driver yet (slow charging), no cameras, and no banking apps, so I keep an Android at home for those. Whether this works for you depends on your phone having a port. reports through the issue forms help, especially for phones that don't work yet.

I think that finally succeeding at having a Linux phone is worth creating a post on HN. I was thinking about a Tell HN but decided to convert the knowledge into a repo so more people can share, discuss, add their phones, new apps, etc. Hope it helps!
